speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Mulroney (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: THE LATE HON. WALTER BAKER TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with true sadness and a deep sense of loss that 1 rise to pay tribute to our colleague, Walter Baker. With Walter's death yesterday, Canada has lost a gifted leader and a distinguished parliamentarian and all of us who knew him have lost a warm and a generous friend.
While new to this House, 1 am not insensitive to its traditions. During the short time that I have been here, I have seen that one of the noblest traditions seems to be the friendship that emerges from the forge of partisan battle. Such friendships, Mr. Speaker, tempered as they often are in the cauldron of debate, are both genuine and durable because, irrespective of Party, they are born in the deep respect that comes from true accomplishment on behalf of Canada.
During one of my first conversations with Walter after my election as Leader, he spoke movingly of his recent visits with the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). Walter told me of the Hon. Member's great contribution to Parliament and to Canada over three decades and how much he would be missed should he decide not to run again. I found it both poignant and elevating, Mr. Speaker, that Walter would speak with such obvious affection for someone of another political Party. I knew that a man capable of such discernment loved people, revered Parliament and ennobled it by his presence.
To earn the respect and the admiration of one's colleagues, including and perhaps particularly those who represent other Parties, is, in my judgment, the ultimate tribute to one's time here. Walter recognized and indeed enjoyed the partisan nature of the House. He understood its rules and he stood in respect of its customs. But Walter sensed as well a growing estrangement of ordinary Canadians from this place he loved so well and served so admirably. He knew that vitriol was no substitute for vigorous debate; that partisanship did not preclude decency; and that humour, true humour, was an instrument to disarm and not a club to embarrass. He was the antithesis of the "merchants of discourtesy" so scorned by Churchill for debasing exchange in another Parliament.
So along with many here he worked tirelessly in the cause of parliamentary reform. The committee of which he was vicechairman produced ten reports, all unanimous, all arrived at by consensus and all designed to improve the parliamentary life of Canada. Time and time again he warned that our rules must be more responsive, our procedures less arcane and our
conduct more becoming, failing which Canadians would progressively question both our relevance and our value.
We should ensure, Mr. Speaker, that his gentle but incisive words not go unheeded. We should learn from his thoughtful personal conduct. We should remember him as a man of distinction who asked only that we refurbish the reputation of this historic place by conducting ourselves with the same sense of courtesy and responsibility we would wish to have associated with our professional careers or our private lives. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, Walter Baker was a great parliamentarian, but above all, he was a gentleman. He had great affection for this place and affection and admiration for all who work here, without regard for political orientation. He was a loyal Member of his Party, but he was never blindly partisan. He saw the qualities of his political adversaries and respected them, and during the short time that I have been in this House, I have always observed that the feeling was mutual. [English]
Above all, Mr. Speaker, Walter Baker loved Canada. He loved it as a country of opportunity and a land of tolerance. He worked tirelessly toward its unity and its enhancement.
In all of the years that 1 knew Walter, I suppose that most of all 1 was always struck by his sense of fairness and by his sense of humour. Problems were to be solved but always with concern for those affected by the decisions. Positions were to be held strongly but always with openness for those of different views.

Ideas were to be put forward, but never with the cool brashness of people who think they have a monopoly on the truth. [English]
Choices were to be made but never with malice toward those of other persuasions.
So today, Mr. Speaker and colleagues, we salute Walter Baker and we say goodbye to a wonderful friend, a man with a unique love of Parliament, a delightful, happy individual of unfailing grace who loved Canada and enriched us all by his presence. On behalf of my Party and 1 am sure on behalf of all Members, I convey to Lois and the family our heartfelt sadness and our deepest condolences.

speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: THE LATE HON. WALTER BAKER TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was with great dismay that we learned late yesterday of the untimely passing of our friend and fellow Member, the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton, the Hon. Walter

November 14, 1983
The Late Hon. W. Baker
Baker, my distinguished predecessor as President of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada.
While we were all aware of the insidious disease which he had been battling since last summer, it appeared from his good spirits and hearty demeanour that he was winning. Therefore, it was a double blow to learn so suddenly of his death.
Walter Baker loved this place. He loved it from the moment he first stepped into the visitors' gallery. From his earliest days as a Member, he demonstrated that he had spent most of his life preparing himself for it. He was a servant of the House, both as Leader of the Government and as Opposition House Leader. More recently he served as vice-chairman of the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure and became one of the most constructive influences on the operations of that Committee by consensus rather than by confrontation.
He was totally committed to the improvement of the institutions of democracy in Canada and as such served as a major contributor to the access to information law.
The people of Nepean-Carleton will miss him greatly. Walter Baker was not just a great parliamentarian, he was a great constituency man. Regardless of political affiliation, there was probably no resident of his district who could find anything but praise for his service to them.
The loss is hardest, however, for his wife, his three young children and his two tiny grandchildren. Walter always spoke of his family with pride and affection. We offer them our most sincere condolences.

Although 1 often had occasion to consult with the Hon. Walter Baker at our meetings of parliamentary House leaders, it was especially during the historic debate on the Constitution that I learned to appreciate my distinguished predecessor in the position of President of the Privy Council. I found his attitude positive, constructive and respectful. A man of "unfailing grace", as the previous speaker said so well, Walter Baker was a typical example of the parliamentarian this institution needs if it is to renew itself and provide better safeguards for our rights and freedoms. This loss will be felt by each and every one of us, and on behalf of the Government, I wish to offer his wife and his entire family our sincere sympathy.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
maintopic: THE LATE HON. WALTER BAKER TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very sad this morning to hear of the passing of Walter Baker. I came to know Walter quite well in the short time I have been in the House of Commons. I came not only to know him when he was House Leader for the Government but also to know him outside Parliament. He was a man of very deep commitment, and he showed at all times a very genuine concern for his constituents on the one hand and for the institution of Parliament on the other. He was firm in his convictions, yet he was gentle in his approach. He was quick to challenge when he felt that you were wrong, but he was equally quick to come to
your defence or to offer words of encouragement if you were under pressure or if you felt that you needed his support.
He clearly felt very deeply for the people of Nepean-Carleton. It has been said by many-and it has been said to me frequently-that we could always find Walter in the constituency. He was known by everyone. He attended every event, large or small. Every family felt touched by him and every family felt confident about Walter.
I remember an occasion when I was invited to speak in Walter's constituency and he noted an advertisement in the newspaper. He sent me a small clipping of the history of the constituency, providing me with some background, with a note just letting me know that he was happy I was going to be there. On another occasion, when my executive assistant was helping to organize a tenants' association, Walter phoned- although we were on different sides of the House-to offer his support and his encouragement, both of which he demonstrated frequently during the period of time when the organization was taking place.
He was committed to his wife and family. I recall going with Walter and his wife to Halifax where I saw a different side of Walter Baker. After the day's work was finished and the arguments had been put aside for the day, I saw the joyous side of Walter, dancing, singing, happy and sharing his happiness with the other people who were at that particular conference.
Walter will be remembered as a person of substance. He will be remembered fondly by his supporters and by his political adversaries alike. He will be remembered by those of us in the House of Commons for his work, as was said earlier, on the parliamentary reform committee. He believed that Parliament could be reformed to be a more meaningful place, and that came through at every meeting which we held when I was a member of that committee. He will be remembered by many for his work on freedom of information. There will be a lasting benefit to the people of Canada as a result of Walter's commitment to this cause.
Walter, of course, will be remembered by his family as a truly decent man. He was taken in the prime of his life but what he left behind will be remembered by everyone. His influence will be with us for years to come. I want to say on behalf of my good friend and colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)-who unfortunately could not be here today-on behalf of my Leader and on behalf of our caucus, how sad we are at his passing. We want to say to his family that they should be proud of the accomplishments of their father, son, grandfather, husband; proud of Walter Baker.

maintopic: THE LATE HON. WALTER BAKER TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to contribute very briefly to the eloquent tributes paid to Walter Baker by my Leader and others who have spoken. For most of my time in this Parliament, Walter Baker was at my side as Acting Prime Minister and as House Leader in Gov-
November 14, 1983

ernment and in Opposition. I counted on him, not just for his industry and judgment, but because he was the most open and vital of men.
Walter loved his work, not just in Parliament, not just in his constituency, but wherever in the country that work carried him. He had the gift of making Government and Parliament personal. He leaves one kind of legacy in the debates and the rules of this Parliament and in the laws which he affected, but for those of us who were privileged to work with him, his larger legacy is the committed, generous, positive spirit which guided everything he did, even in the days when disease was pulling him down.
More than a colleague, even more than a friend, he was a constant example of the decency, generosity and love which are at the heart of the way we live. We miss him, we mourn him, and our hearts go out to Lois and to his family.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: THE LATE HON. WALTER BAKER TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER
speechtext:
I wonder if 1 could be permitted at this point to join in the respect being paid to a man whom 1 have known for over 25 years and counted as a very good friend.
Walter was born in Cardinal, and practised law in Ottawa before coming to this place in association with the Hon. Dick Bell who was a Member for Carleton. Walter succeeded to that seat in 1972.
Members of the House have paid tribute to Walter as a parliamentarian and words cannot express his love for this place, his contribution and his work in the direction of parliamentary reform.
Words have also been said about his work as a constituency representative. Walter represented a constituency adjacent to my own. We had many occasions on which we acted jointly, always in a spirit of good friendship, with frank and free exchange of opinion where there were differences, but always with mutual respect and, I would like to think, affection.
Walter's family life was also a model. In days when people are sometimes disrespectful of those who hold public office, Walter Baker was a man no one could possibly criticize. His eminent virtue, his industry, his integrity and his warm human qualities made him very much endeared as a friend. I personally wish to express my sympathy to Lois and members of his family. This has been a difficult period for all of them. I hope it is some comfort to her and to them to know of the deep affection and admiration we held for Walter.

maintopic: THE LATE HON. WALTER BAKER TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker last night I was both astonished and saddened at the news of the death of our colleague, the Hon. Walter Baker. On behalf of all the Members of the Special Committee on Procedure and Organization, a committee I have been privileged to chair and on which 1 was also privileged to work together with Mr. Baker in his capacity as Vice-Chairman, I wish to offer our sincere sympathy to his wife Lois and all his
The Late Hon. W. Baker
children. It was a very rewarding experience to work with an experienced parliamentarian like Walter Baker. I am sure that his passing will be felt as a tremendous loss, not only by the members of his family but by his constituents and the Parliament of Canada.

There is no doubt that Walter Baker's work, his concern and his commitment had a great deal to do with the quality of the reports produced by the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure. This Committee provided me with the unique opportunity of working with a great parliamentarian in the person of Walter Baker. Throughout his career Mr. Baker and I, when we sat on both Government and Opposition sides, occupied different positions in the House where we had to adopt and defend Party positions. Never once in all those times did the work we carried out on behalf of our Party policies ever interfere with his honour, integrity and the feeling of friendship that he had with myself and many other MPs. We shall miss him, and this institution will be the lesser for his regrettable passing away.

maintopic: THE LATE HON. WALTER BAKER TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a constituent of Walter Baker and a long time friend, I would like to add my personal tribute to his family and himself at this time.
You mentioned that he was born in Cardinal, which is indicative of the fact that he came from the Valley. He also knew that I was married to a woman whose family goes back to the original settlers of theValley, going back to the veterans of the Napoleonic wars. He constantly came to me to talk about the roots and the views of these people because he knew I had some knowledge of the history of the County of Carle-ton. It was his deep understanding of these people which carried him through many a decision. He had a deep appreciation of the background of these English, Scots and Irish who came here after the great wars in Europe to settle the land, break the ground and clear the bush.
Even though I lived on the outskirts of his riding in Mano-tick, almost every week he would ask me: "What are the bus drivers saying?" This was our way of learning through the school children what was going on in the homes.
I think that background should be put on the record because Walter in his public life was not only interested in the affairs of the nation, but he was interested in the views, feelings and hopes and aspirations of every person in the whole area he represented. As was said before, he was the kind of Member of Parliament that all of us would like to be. Along with others here, my sympathy goes to the family.

Mr. Speaker, I have the temerity to rise at this time not to add to the excellent expressions of tribute which have been made, because my words could not do that, but to try to suggest that words can now be brought into action. Perhaps our concerns as we have expressed them concerning our affection and love for

November 14, 1983
The Late Hon. W. Baker
Walter Baker may in this case be put into action by a non-partisan approach to the subject of parliamentary reform, which was so dear to him. I hope this event will provide us with that added incentive to make a reality that which was such a part of his life's work.
The second way in which we might be able to express our feelings, those of us who are not given an opportunity to take part in this tribute, is to ask that before this period is brought to an end and we begin Orders of the Day, we might have an opportunity to stand for a moment of silence together.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: THE LATE HON. WALTER BAKER TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday evening I was returning home by car from a Latvian function commemorating the sixty-fifth anniversary of the proclamation of the independence of Latvia. The Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) knows which function I am speaking of because he was the keynote speaker. As I pulled into the driveway 1 heard the announcement over the radio and I stopped the car halfway up the driveway and my first words were, "Oh no, not Walter."
We did lose a great parliamentarian and I would like to take this opportunity to express sympathy to his wife and children on behalf of Canadians of Estonian, Lithuanian and Latvian descent. 1 think most of us sitting in this Chamber know that every year we have a function here called the Baltic Evening. Walter always co-chaired that evening with a Senator. 1 know Canadians of Estonian, Latvian and Lithuanian descent would want me to express condolences to Walter's entire family.
Just last summer young Lithuanians from around the world were having a conference in Canada, with a one-day program here in Ottawa. They were looking for someone on the Government side and someone from the Official Opposition to co-chair this function. I called Walter and he immediately said: "Yes, Jesse, no problem." I could not make that function because of my commitment with Bill C-155, but Walter attended. Even though he was getting treatment for his cancer, he gave up the day to join these young Lithuanians from around the world to shake their hands and say hello. That was Walter. He always co-operated.
When we had our Standing Order 43s in the House, I knew that if I ever wanted unanimous consent on any issue dealing with human rights, all I had to do was go to Walter, especially when he was House Leader, and I knew it was granted. On behalf of Canadians from the Baltic States and all Canadians, 1 too wish to add my condolences to the entire Baker family.

maintopic: THE LATE HON. WALTER BAKER TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will speak very briefly because words are difficult. I would like to join in paying tribute to our late colleague. Walter Baker was an outstanding Canadian, a great advocate of this city and a dedicated Member of the House.
His legacy is one of parliamentary reform. I know that he would want that to be ongoing because this institution, as it lives, must be involved in reform. Freedom of information is also an outstanding legacy.
This House has lost a dedicated, outstanding parliamentarian and 1 have lost a friend.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE LATE HON. WALTER BAKER TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is hard to add more to what has already been said here today but I think 1 have to add the words that I have inside of me over the loss that we have experienced with Walter's passing. We all know that Walter was a very highly respected parliamentarian in the House. He was seen as that not only in his riding but in the City of Ottawa and across the country. He loved Canada.
He could always be counted on in the House to add to the debate and add a Canadian and national perspective which had meaning to all of us. He was loved and he loved the people of his constituency. That perspective was always brought to bear when Walter spoke here or when he spoke in his riding.
My constituency, as does yours, Mr. Speaker, borders on Walter's. Like you, when we had joint events which we attended-which was often-Walter could always be counted on to be concerned about the people who were there, what their problems were and how he and I jointly could help those people. He could always be counted on to do so in a totally non-partisan and co-operative fashion. He was a great constituency man and will be greatly missed in his constituency.
When I was first elected, even though Walter came from another Party, he was always at my assistance, counselling me on what it meant to be a Member of Parliament. 1 have learned a great deal from Walter about how 1 could deal with my constituency, better serve my constituents and how I should conduct myself in the House. Walter was a great model for us and a great example for all parliamentarians now and in the future. I hope he will be remembered as such. He was a role model for us. He will be deeply missed as a friend, colleague and national leader. 1 want to express my deep regrets and sympathy to Lois and the family and to let them know that Walter will be fondly remembered here as a model for all of us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 21 I would like to call to the attention of the House that the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has just returned from a trip of immense importance to Canada and the world, a mission of peace to European capitals. The Prime Minister presented four points that are part of a strategy of peace, including a call for a five-power nuclear conference to negotiate nuclear arsenal limits, and the expansion of the non-proliferation treaty. It is encouraging to know that the Prime Minister has returned from Europe with a consensus among leaders there that these peace initiatives should be supported.
The Prime Minister has begun the task of moving the world back from the brink of nuclear holocaust and international tensions which increase the likelihood of war. 1 was moved by his statement yesterday and 1 draw this particularly to the attention of Canadians. He said:
We can without effort abandon our fate to the mindless drift toward nuclear war. Or we can gather our strength .... to turn aside the forces bearing down on us.
Canadians have made great contributions to mankind. Canadians could make no greater contribution now and in the future than working for the preservation of mankind. 1 call upon all Members of this House and all Canadians to support actively the Prime Minister's peace initiatives and his efforts both here in Canada and abroad.

Mr. Speaker, recent discussions about the possibility of Canada participating as a peace-keeper in Grenada brings to mind another peace-keeping role in which this country is involved. I am speaking of Cyprus, where Canada has sent peace-keeping troops for 19 years. Our mandate for maintaining a peace-keeping force in Cyprus comes up for renewal in December. Certainly one cannot and should not advocate a troop withdrawal simply

November 14, 1983
because our peace-keeping role in Cyprus has not brought about a resolution to the country's peace talks. But the stalemate in negotiations is cause for concern.
One has to wonder whether Canadian peace-keeping troops in Cyprus are as much a part of the problem as a part of the solution in that our presence there makes it easier for the stalemate to continue. Some 500 Canadian soldiers are in Cyprus, and most soldiers do a six-month tour of duty. It is a tremendous strain on our manpower and resources, so perhaps the time has come to review carefully our role as peace-keepers in order to ensure that we are as effective as possible.
I therefore suggest a parliamentary review, a white paper on Canada's peace-keeping commitment, with particular emphasis on our role in NATO. Canada has every right to be proud of its reputation as a peace-keeper. However, if we are to maintain that reputation we must ensure that our peace-keeping role is practical and effective.

DAVIE SHIPBUILDING YARD IN QUEBEC-IMPORTANCE OF SETTLING SITUATION QUICKLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the situation at the Davie shipyards remains disastrous. In spite of the contribution of the Canadian government to the construction of the CN Marine ferry in the amount of $121 million and to the repairs of a few other ships, the workers will soon have to face the hard fact that as of mid-1984 there will be nothing on the order book. Nearly 1,000 employees who are already out of work will see their unemployment insurance benefits replaced by welfare payments before Christmas. This problem at the largest employer of the Quebec region must be solve quickly.
Recently, we have heard many comments and questions in this regard and I urge all parties involved to reply to them jointly. First, why have the Davie shipyards lost all the major contracts awarded recently by the Canadian Government, even though the average hourly rate at Davie is lower than at Marine Industries Limited of Sorel, for instance? Second, are the workers satisfied with their productivity? Is there something to prevent Davie from being the lowest bidder for these contracts? Third, does the Quebec Government, through the SGF give unfair support to one shipyard at the defense of another? All interested parties will have to jointly answer everyone of these questions in order to solve this urgent problem.

CALL FOR HOLDING OF GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in August, 1969, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated, "We would be on the road to financial disaster if nothing were done to bring spending under control."
Since that time government spending has increased 693 per cent, and it has cost every Canadian taxpayer over $10,000. The net national debt at the end of the last fiscal year was $119.2 billion, but the Auditor General believes that this has been understated by $14.5 billion. This year interest on the debt will cost each Canadian taxpayer more than $1,700.
The result of all this has been continuing high interest rates, slow economic growth, low productivity, and high unemployment rates. Unemployment Insurance Commission benefits in 1982 were equal to $8.5 billion, more than the combined government spending of the four Atlantic Provinces.
The magazine Euromoney ranks Canada's over-all economic growth since 1974 at sixty-second in the world, our inflation performance is rated twenty-fifth, and our balance of payments performance is rated twentieth. It is an economic record that only a Liberal Government could take pride in, a Liberal Government led by a Prime Minister who has stated unequivocally that he would choose Cuban or Chinese socialism as the national model for Canadian society. But the polls indicate that Canadians have not been fooled. The Prime Minister should call an election now and give them an opportunity to show that Canadians do not choose Cuban, Chinese, Liberal, or any other form of socialism.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been visiting several European capitals as a self-appointed pilgrim of peace, the nuclear arms race, abetted by Canada, continues, and war close to home is imminent.
No matter how highly respected an individual might be in world councils, an individual's globe-trotting efforts are all for naught if his own Government's policies and actions support the nuclear arms race. It is not enough for a political leader to go on a peace-making mission if his Government's policies do not fulfil basic peace-making objectives.
While the Prime Minister talks nuclear age peace, Canada continues to prepare to test nuclear weapons delivery vehicles for the United States Air Force. And while the Prime Minister implores other Governments to abandon the nuclear arms race, Canada, thanks to federal financial subsidies, builds components for new nuclear weapons systems. Canada must, itself, practise nuclear arms restraint if the Prime Minister is to be a credible messenger of peace.
Finally, the Prime Minister rightly deplores the increasing use of violence in international affairs, yet says nothing about the imminence of war on our very doorstep in Central America. The escalating U.S. military presence in the region, and the mounting threat of a U.S. backed invasion of Nicaragua, demand a firm and immediate protest from Canada. We wait anxiously for changes in the Government's nuclear arms policies, and we wait anxiously for Canada's efforts to prevent a U.S. inspired war in our own hemisphere.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Premier of Quebec has taken a new tack by revealing in advance the contents of the mini-budget to be brought down tomorrow evening by the Quebec Minister of Finance, Mr. Jacques Parizeau.
Interestingly, the leader of the Quebec Government managed to announce a spectacular recovery plan while at the same time giving Quebecers the impression that the federal
Government had not played a role in creating many jobs in this province.
Mr. Levesque wants to speed economic recovery without, however, getting rid of the factors that inhibit investment. The House will recall that the Leader of the Quebec Government did not announce he was repealing the anti-scab law, that the sliding tax on gas would be removed, that he would be maintaining special tax measures to make Quebec more attractive than Ontario for business executives, or that municipalities would be allowed to accept grants from the federal Government.
Mr. Speaker, the principal obstacle to genuine economic recovery in Quebec remains, and that is the ongoing, neurotic concern for independence the Levesque Government maintains today and will continue to maintain as the main element of its party program.
As was pointed out not long ago by our Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), for every job we create, we lose three every time the Government of Quebec talks about independence.
Mr. Speaker, we can only hope the Premier of Quebec will give the question some thought and finally give Quebecers the Government they deserve.

ACTION URGED TO CONTROL GASOLINE EMISSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, automobile exhaust contains gases called nitrogen oxides. These turn into nitric acid in the air and contribute in a significant way to acid rain. It is disturbing to me and to many of my constituents in Parry Sound-Muskoka, as well as to other people throughout the country, that our gas emissions are three times higher than those permitted in the United States. Does this not make it easier for the Americans to point an accusing finger at us? Who are we to complain about them when we are unwilling to cut our gas emissions?
I urge the Government to initiate and approve legislation in this regard to bring our gas emissions into line with United States standards. I also urge that this action be considered for the 1985 automobile model year and that both Ministers responsible, Environment and Transport, present the seriousness of this to their cabinet colleagues.

subsubtopic: CONVERSION OF CUSTOMS TARIFF TO METRIC MEASURE
speechtext: Is it intended to convert tourist exemption provisions of the Customs Tariff to metric measure and, if so, what will be the date of the change?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: CONVERSION OF CUSTOMS TARIFF TO METRIC MEASURE
speechtext:
Bill C-90, which was approved by Parliament on December 16, 1982, provides the Government with the authority to introduce the metric system into the Customs Tariff by Order in Council. Officials of the Department of Finance have begun drafting amendments to the Customs Tariff in consultation with interested parties, including officials in this Department. Imperial measures which appear in the personal exemption tariff items will be converted to metric within the next few months.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
1.	Does the Department of Communications plan to encourage international standards on magnetic compatibility between telephones and hearing aids and, if so, in what manner?
2.	Has TAPAC indicated its willingness to deal with questions of compatibility between hearing aids and the telephone?
3.	Does TAPAC have any mechanism for consulting with hearing impaired consumers and, if so, what is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext:
In so far
as the Department of Communications is concerned, the reply to the above question is as follows:
1.	The Department of Communications (DOC) has supported and will continue to support the development of domestic and international standards or mechanisms which will ensure universal access to the telephone networks by hearing-impaired persons. Canadian industries and laboratories, with the assistance of DOC, also actively participate in various domestic, North American and international activities. As an example, participation in The International Electrotechnical Commission and the Electronic Industries Association is aimed at finding technical solutions to the problems encountered by hearing-aid users.
2.	As encouraged by the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) in its Telecom Decision 82-14 regarding the attachment of subscriber-provided terminal equipment to the networks of the federally regulated common carriers, the Terminal Attachment Program Advisory Committee (TAPAC) is monitoring domestic and international technical developments in order to assess additional means by which the access of hearing-impaired persons to telephone service can be improved. TAPAC is primarily involved in the development of technical standards for telecommunications equipment which is connected to the public switched telephone network; such standards must ensure adequate protection to the network against potential harm. To the extent that compatibility standards relate to network protec-
November 14, 1983

tion, TAPAc would be mandated to deal with this particular
issue.
3.	Hearing-impaired consumers or any other interested party may make representations to TAPAC or attend TAPAC meetings as a mechanism for consulting.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: 1 ask, Mr. Speaker, that the remaining questions be allowed to stand.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the Parliamentary Secretary to a question I asked on June 1, 1981. The question is No. 2,568. It is a very simple question. It reads:
What was the increase in real terms in the Department of National Defence's expenditures, including statutory costs and expressed in percentages, for each fiscal year 1970-71 to 1979-80?
In budget terms it means that question is three years old and I would have thought that in three years the Department would have been able to figure out how much it spent even in the most recent of these years. Would the Parliamentary Secretary be kind enough to chase that question up?
At the same time, to make his day, 1 would like to tell the Parliamentary Secretary that starred question No. 4,336 about which I have spoken to him several times and which has been on the Order Paper for a year and a half, has now been resolved outside of this jurisdiction. 1 would like that question withdrawn from the Order Paper.

Mr. Speaker, I would also draw the attention of the Parliamentary Secretary to question No. 3,216 which 1 asked on October 23, 1981. It reads:
Did the Prime Minister travel to New York in March 1981 and, if so, what was the total cost of the trip and what percentage will be paid by the taxpayer?
Could the Parliamentary Secretary indicate now after three years whether there is any particular reason why his office could not have given this information?

Just two years.

I am not sure what the procedure is concerning the request that question No. 4,336 be withdrawn from the Order Paper. I think we have to go through the Chair or the Table Officers for that.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is related to this question?

Yes, Mr. Speaker. Could the Parliamentary Secretary explain to the House why it would take a year and a half for the Government to answer a starred question which, by tradition in this place, is not only answered orally but on an urgent basis?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: In 48 hours, it used to be.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, here we go around that mulberry bush again.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is a Grit bush.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As we have indicated before and in looking through the precedents, there is no precedent that a starred question is treated any differently from another question other than the fact that when the answer is given it is read orally in the House. That is what Beauchesne says and that is the precedent that has been before this House.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Rubbish.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is no precedent whatsoever that requires that a starred question be answered on any more urgent basis than any other question. The Government tries to give as urgent attention to these questions as possible in order to get answers back to Members. We have up to this point answered 85 per cent of all questions that have been asked. I think that is a very good record for the Government, Mr. Speaker. Certainly we will do our best to make sure that all these other questions are answered as soon as they possibly can.

Mr. Speaker, as we are talking about the question I asked which had to do with a lieutenant the Department of National Defence was refusing to readmit to the reserves, let me say that I took the matter up with two Ministers and two Parliamentary Secretaries and the problem was eventually resolved to my satisfaction.
I care little whether the question is withdrawn by a motion of mine, by unanimous consent or by waiting for this interminable session to end, because the question will disappear from the Order Paper one way or the other.

speechtext: Is there unanimous consent for the Hon. Member for Victoria to withdraw from the Order Paper the question to which he has made reference?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, my point of order is a follow-up to the original point 1 raised with the Parliamentary Secretary. The Prime Minister's trip was almost three years ago. I asked the question a little over two years ago. Is the Parliamentary Secretary aware that in our frustration we went to the access to information and privacy co-ordinator of the Privy Council office? His officials have now informed us that the Prime Minister's trip in 1981 cost $5,607.75. If he is aware of that,

The thrust of my question is whether the information that we now have, the $5,607.75 cost given to us by the co-ordination for access to information and privacy, is correct, or is there some information to be added to his report? speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on the point of order which was addressed by the Parliamentary Secretary a moment ago with respect to the practice of answering starred questions. The Parliamentary Secretary, who seems to view this whole exercise of denying information to Parliament very gleefully, would not in my view know a precedent if he tripped over it, like he does with most things, if he would get his nose out of Beauschesne and out of the Standing Orders and go back over the debates of this House, he would learn that starred questions were, at one point, before the changes for the worse were brought about by the practices of the present Government, answered in 48 hours. At the very latest, they were answered in three days. That has been the practice in this place. He and 1 have had this exchange before. Madam Speaker has taken it under advisement. She was going to look at it and get back to us. You, Mr. Speaker, have been around here long enough to appreciate the significance of starred questions. They do have some significance. The significance that attaches to them is that any normal self-respecting Government would treat them as urgent and bring forward the answers on an urgent basis, not hide them for a year and a half, as in the case of the question of the Hon. Member for Victoria. Otherwise, there is no purpose for starred questions. They are there for a purpose, the purpose is urgency. Rather than changing the practice, we should abide with past practices and distinguish urgent questions from those which require in some cases volumes of
statistical information which takes time to produce. A question as simple as the one the Hon. Member for Victoria starred certainly could have been answered within three days, but was not.

speakerposition: Deputy Opposition Whip; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on somewhat the same point of order to ask the Parliamentary Secretary about Question No. 5,038 regarding the number of ships permitted into Canada under special authority to participate in offshore oil exploration.
The question was starred because it was anticipated that the Government would in fact add additional revenues to the PIPS Program. We noted today in the House the question by the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre and the response by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. If we had had the answer that 1 sought on September 21, we would have been in a much better position to evaluate the Minister's response to the Hon. Member.
In the years that I have spent in this Chamber, the practice of starred questions was to identify those questions which Members felt were urgent, topical or pertained to business either before the House or shortly to come before the House. speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre De Bane (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
that Bill C-170, An Act to authorize investment in and the provision of financial assistance to the Atlantic Fisheries for the purpose of restructuring certain fishery enterprises, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.
He said: Mr. Speaker, speaking on second reading of Bill C-170, I wish to seek the support of the House for this Bill. I would say it is not merely a Bill but a historic milestone, if we consider the impact the legislation will have on the future of our Atlantic fisheries. I would even go so far as to say that this Bill is as important as the Fisheries Act and the measures taken in 1977 to extend our jurisdiction over fisheries to the 200-mile zone.
This legislation must also be seen within the historical context of our Atlantic fisheries, part of which goes back several decades, while another part has materialized during the last six months. Mr. Speaker, 1 do not intend to dwell at length on past history. Nevertheless, I think we could usefully review some aspects of the history of our Atlantic fisheries over the last ten years, to illustrate the sequence of events that has brought us to the present situation, and to explain how the
measures that are about to be taken by the Government of Canada, with, we hope, the support of all parties of this House, are a logical consequence thereof.
First, a quick look at our Atlantic fisheries at the beginning of the seventies. Hon. Members will recall that at the time, the fisheries were in a crisis situation as they are today. Foreign fishing fleets were devastating the fish stocks off our coasts. The abundant stocks of groundfish that had been the mainstay of the fishing industry for generations were threatened with depletion. The federal Government was called in and provided very substantial assistance in keeping the industry afloat, as it were.
We were aware that the fish stocks that formed a vital part of our economy in the Atlantic provinces were in very serious danger. We were also aware that this was due to uncontrolled fishing. On the basis of our experience of international controls, we knew that the only answer to these problems lay in establishing Canadian sovereignty over these resources.
Let us now look at the year 1977, when Canada proclaimed its authority over the 200-mile zone and we started on the long and difficult task of rebuilding the resource that forms the basis of this industry.
We find our next historic milestone in more recent years, namely, 1981, when our country had been exercising control over fish stocks within the 200-mile zone for five years. I think we may be proud of the manner in which we have discharged this responsibility. Our success both in safeguarding and reestablishing fish stocks is undisputed and worthy of mention. In fact, our achievements in this area have been cited the world over, and rightly so, as prime examples of excellent fisheries resource management. In 1981, however, we were once again facing a very serious situation in the Atlantic fisheries. Companies were on the verge of bankruptcy, fishermen and processing plant workers were laid off or about to be, shareholders were worried and businessmen reluctant to invest. However, there was no shortage of fish, there was no overfishing by foreign fleets and no operation of factory ships beyond our control.
There is a paradox here that is clear to even the most superficial observer. Here we have an industry that is fortunate in being able to draw on some of the richest fisheries resources of the whole world. It is located nearer the United States, one of the main markets for this product, than any of its competitors. We have people whose fishing and ocean-going traditions are as good if not better than anyone else's. We have a country that since 1978, in terms of volume, has become the biggest exporter of fish and Fish products. Nevertheless, the industry was once again in dire straits and in danger of disappearing once and for all.
The obvious question is: How can an industry that has so much going for it manage to get itself into such serious trouble? More than once, my predecessor at the Department
November 14, 1983

of Fisheries and Oceans reminded the industry that by extending our jurisdiction, we had acquired new borders but lost one excuse. We could no longer blame our problems on overfishing by foreign fleets, and so if our problems continued and would not go away, we would have to change our own procedures. In other words, we would have to look at the problem from within.
Mr. Speaker, it was clear that we now had an entirely different situation. Financial assistance would have been justified when there was overfishing by foreign fleets. However, in the 80s, this reason was no longer valid. The time had come to define our international problems and try to correct them. That is why the Government established the Atlantic Fisheries Task Force headed by Mr. Michael Kirby. As Hon. Members are aware, the terms of reference of the task force were not only to describe the symptoms but to establish the cause of the disease. Furthermore, this could not be done in a vacuum but required frequent consultation with industry, fishermen, and the provincial governments concerned.
The task force made its report early this year. Its findings were sobering and instructive, but they were also basically very positive, very upbeat. As other studies before it have indicated repeatedly, this one found that whatever Atlantic fisheries might lack, they were very rich in potential. This, the task force confirmed, is a Canadian asset of immense and renewable value. The task force also found-and observers within and outside the Government have agreed with the finding- that although external influences were involved, the industry's problems were structural. They stemmed from inherent defects and internal causes. The boat had not capsized just because of the storm; it capsized because it was not built to withstand heavy weather.
Since early this year, as Hon. Members know, the Government, along with the Governments of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, the large deep sea companies and financial institutions, has been attempting to come up with a plan to keep the industry afloat. In the Province of Quebec the large co-op, United Fishermen, which has for the last two years been promised financial assistance by the Quebec Government, at the end rightly despaired. So it came and struck a deal with my Department also.
The agreements we have reached with Newfoundland and Nova Scotia and with this large co-op in the Province of Quebec reflect to some extent the recommendations made by the task force. They envisage work on many fronts.
To what extent, Mr. Minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
If the Hon. Member would just give me the chance to finish my speech, I will gladly answer any questions he may have.
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
Aren't you going to answer that in your speech? It is very important.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
The partners in these consultations agree that the industry needs to change. It needs to improve its marketing arrangements. It needs to become leaner and more efficient ashore and afloat. However, more basically, it needs to be a different kind of industry. It is not enough to beach the existing vessel and patch it up for another voyage. The industry needs a new design, one with enough built-in strength and stability to stay afloat even when the economic barometer falls.
The Bill which 1 have the honour to bring before the House represents one major step in that process. In the course of long, sometimes difficult negotiations this year, I reached agreements with the Governments of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, with the industry and with financial institutions on a plan to reorganize or restructure, as the Bill puts it, the Atlantic fisheries.
The plan calls for, among other things, a substantial investment of Canadian taxpayers' money. The purpose of the Bill is to authorize the federal Government to play a major part in a co-operative effort to restructure the industry. Specifically, it would authorize the Government of Canada to invest in the industry and to make loan guarantees.
Before discussing the Bill itself, I want to tell Hon. Members why the legislation is necessary and desirable. Of course, the most basic reason is that without action the industry will go under. There is a funding vacuum. No private investors have come forward to fill it. Given the industry's present financial state, it is simply not able to take that kind of risk.
Fet me begin my review of the situation with Newfoundland. All observers, Government and private, agree that without exception the deep sea processing companies in that Province are in a state of terminal financial distress. Several at this point are already in receivership. As Hon. Members know, the Governments of Newfoundland and Canada signed an agreement on measures to restructure the Newfoundland deep sea industry. The agreement was not easy to achieve, but we have it now. It was signed in an atmosphere of cordiality and united resolve. I understand that the Government of Newfoundland and labrador is at the moment discussing in the legislature of that Province a Bill, the object of which is to ratify the agreement which has been reached between our two Governments. I might add that it has been hailed by the Premier of that Province as the most important bilateral agreement reached between that Province and the central Government since its entry into Canada in 1949. I am happy to note that, like all other major achievements in Newfoundland, it was done under a Fiberal Government in Ottawa.
What our Governments hoped to accomplish together is summed up very concisely in the preamble to that agreement. That document says, Mr. Speaker, that our objective is to find a just and lasting solution for the rebuilding of the deep sea

November 14, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act fishery, one which recognizes the fundamental role which the fishing industry plays in Newfoundland and Labrador.
In the course of consultations which led to this agreement, practical measures were agreed upon by both Governments and by the financial institutions which will provide part of the funding. It was agreed specifically that the logical and effective course would be to combine the assets of John Penny and Sons, the Lake Group Limited, North Atlantic Fisheries, Fishery Products and some other companies. Certain assets of H. B. Nickerson and Sons in Nova Scotia would be merged with these Newfoundland elements to achieve a balanced mix of products.
In our opinion, and those of our partners in these consultations, this would produce the basic structure for an economically viable company-lean, efficient and able to compete with any fishing nation in the world. One component of the new structure would be an operating company. The other would be a holding company.
In Nova Scotia we have reached an agreement in principle with the provincial Government and with the Bank of Nova Scotia. In this case we are talking about consolidation of two main elements. National Sea Products and certain parts of the H. B. Nickerson and Sons operations, into a restructured National Sea Products Company. In this case, financing will be achieved by conversion of some debt to equity by the Bank of Nova Scotia and by the Province, and injection of new cash for equity by the Government of Canada.
A presentation was made to the board of directors of National Sea Products on October 17 on behalf of the federal and Nova Scotia Governments and the Bank of Nova Scotia, proposing a merging into National Sea Products of certain Nova Scotia fishing assets of H. B. Nickerson and Sons. This proposal includes provisions for an estimated $90 million of common share equity to restructure the balance sheet of National Sea Products. The equity is to be provided by a consortium composed of the two Governments and the bank through a company which will, as a result, probably own in excess of 75 per cent of the common shares of the restructured National Sea Products. The exact percentage will depend on the price at which the new common shares will be issued.
As Hon. Members will know, National Sea is a publicly-owned company with publicly-traded shares. The board of directors of that firm is considering the proposal submitted to it and will be seeking the approval of its shareholders for any recommended response. I should also add that discussions and negotiations have taken place which will result in the sale of the total H. B. Nickerson and Sons interests in fish processing operations in Atlantic Canada-including a controlling interest in National Sea Products-to a company owned by the two Governments and the Bank of Nova Scotia. The Nickerson assets located in Newfoundland, plus the Riverport, Nova Scotia facilities and 12 scallop vessels, will be transferred to a company to be incorporated in Newfoundland as per the agreement made between the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador on September 26, 1983.
I remain hopeful that we can secure full agreement of all parties involved in the Nova Scotia restructuring plant in the near future, and that implementation of the agreements can proceed.

With respect to Quebec, the situation is quite different. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, we have in the Province a huge co-operative-Pecheurs-Unis-which represents close to 50 per cent of plant workers of Quebec's fishing industry and accounts for nearly 40 per cent of catches in terms of volume. As everyone knows, for two years now this leading co-operative which is affiliated to the Desjardins group has been promised by the provincial Government that it will solve those problems and provide assistance. The simple truth is that in the past two years the Canadian Government, represented by my predecessor the former Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) and myself since last year, has made it possible to rescue Pecheurs-Unis during the last two fishing seasons, those of 1982 and 1983, twice in a row. In my opinion, the Pecheurs-Unis case is one of the most telling examples of Canadian federalism. Those fishermen and plant workers had been told by the provincial Government that it would help them and solve their problems, but they finally realized that if they really wanted action, if they really wanted a solution, they had to ask the Canadian Government. However, I must admit that certain aspects of the Pecheurs-Unis case remain unclear to this day. Under extreme circumstances, one can understand why the Government of Quebec would refuse to shoulder its responsibilities, but what is impossible to understand is why that Government not only denied help to Pecheurs-Unis but did everything it could to destroy, even to the extent of questioning the personal integrity of their leaders, even questioning the personal integrity of one of the senior Desjardins officials. The Government even made references to police investigations and threatened fishermen who sought the assistance of the Canadian Government with the loss of their rights-and these are Quebec taxpayers-which belong to all Quebec fishermen.
Why is that? Mr. Speaker, I confess that I do not understand, just as the fishermen and those who looked into the case of Pecheurs-Unis do not understand either. In any event, the Canadian Government did rescue Pecheurs-Unis during the last two fishing seasons. Should anyone ask me why, I would answer simply that it was our duty to intervene.
History will note that in the case of all those commercial undertakings which I mentioned-National Sea Products Ltd., Nickerson, Fishery Products, Penny & Sons, North Atlantic, Pecheurs-Unis-hundreds and thousands of creditors agreed to wait and did not take any action because they knew that we were trying to find a solution. The one and only creditor who behaved like a common finance company and who seized the assets was the Quebec government. The one and only creditor! Of course, I could not let this opportunity pass by without
November 14, 1983

thanking all the creditors, large and small, who have demonstrated considerable patience over the past two years, especially towards the Pecheurs Unis, and I am sure I am speaking on behalf of all hon. members when 1 say that 1 cannot understand how the Quebec government, which is supposed to be closer to the taxpayers, could be, of all the creditors, the only one to seize the assets of the Pecheurs Unis. And as everybody knows, it seized Madelipeche, a plant, most shares of which belonged to the Pecheurs Unis.
I have examined the contract which the Quebec government had forced at the time upon the Pecheurs Unis whereby, for all practical purposes, the Quebec government was buying the Madelipeche assets for a ridiculously low price. Mr. Speaker, you have there an example of the great social conscience of the Quebec government. It has done something which no financial company would have dared. In so doing, the Quebec government has attacked the personal integrity of the Pecheurs Unis leaders as well as the Desjardins movement, and it has passed a legislation to take over the assets of the Pecheurs Unis; it has even threatened the fishermen and the plant workers with retaliation if they accepted the offer of the Canadian government, and in spite of all the threats and intimidation tactics, I am happy to report that all those concerned, namely, the fishermen, the unions, the plant workers, the creditors and the leaders of the Desjardins movement, have accepted the offer of the Canadian Government. As evidence of this, I should like to read into the official report the letter which Mr. Pierre Lefebvre, my Assistance Deputy Minister in charge of the Pecheurs Unis file, has just received from Mr. Jean-Paul Paradis, the fisherman who is the President of the Pecheurs Unis of Quebec, and I quote:
Dear Assistant Deputy Minister;
I have acquainted myself with the results of the 2nd Information Meeting which was held with you in Newport last Tuesday evening, and I feel that these results are very satisfactory.
I emphasize the words "very satisfactory", Mr. Speaker.
Some 25 fishermen in attendance thus reasserted their agreement to the restructuring plan of the Canadian government, which means that they do not question the value of the first consultation in which they had taken part last October 19.
Up to now, the official and private consultations going on in Newport indicate and lead us to conclude that a major part of the local fleet still supports your restructuring proposal.
Indeed, we are speaking about a cooperative where each member has one vote.
In addition, the members of fisheries cooperatives throughout the northern Gaspe area still maintain their acceptance of your plan, while our organized workers continue to have a very favourable response.
However, some confusion seems to subsist as to the firm desire of your government to proceed with this plan, which confusion is encouraged by those who oppose it.
I therefore wish to reaffirm our full and complete acceptance of your offer as made last October 16 in Gaspe, and I sincerely hope that you will submit in the near future the contractual agreement sealing the transaction through which the assets of Pecheurs-Unis will be transferred to a new corporation, still to be
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
established and in which your government will probably have a majority of shares.
Sincerely yours,
Jean-Paul Paradis Chairman
Pecheurs-Unis du Quebec
I would like to say to the chairman of Pecheurs-Unis, as well as to all the fishermen, all the plant workers, the unions, the Desjardin movement, the small and the large creditors, all those who stood up to the threats, the blackmail, the overstatements-and I see that my hon. predecessor is coming in, he who has done so much in relation with Pecheurs-Unis-I would like to tell all those people who stood up to all that and to these attacks on their reputation, that the Canadian government will not abandon them and that we shall do exactly as promised by my predecessor, the Hon. Minister of Public Works. We are going to act and to establish this corporation which will also make its marketing services available to all other Quebec businesses. When I think that this is being called an ideological conflict! Mr. Speaker, we only have to look at what was done in the case of Madelipeche. This company was not seized, taken over or appropriated to be given back to the people of the Magdalen Islands. The Quebec government appropriated the company for itself. This goes much deeper; we might as well recognize that it is an ideological conflict. The Quebec government is refusing to behave as a government which favours dialogue. As avidence, the Canadian Saltfish Corporation Act provides for one representative to be designated by the Quebec government to defend the Quebec viewpoint. That seat is still vacant, and this goes to prove to what extent the Quebec Government is ranking its ideology above the welfare of its fishermen.
The case at hand is a good example of how much federalism benefits Quebec fishermen more than 95 per cent of whom have supported the Canadian Government program that was sprinkled with no threats, arm-twisting or upmanship. When 1 think of the Quebec Minister of Fisheries and Minister of Agriculture going to Riviere-au-Tonnerre to offer them $800,000, ten times more than he offered last year! This is what he offered them to try and get their support. Despite everything, I invite them for the last time to accept the Canadian Government's offer and become a shareholder as all other partners did, in that new organization which we are going to set up.
Some elements of restructuring the Atlantic fishery are specific to the Provinces involved but some are common to all, and I would like to touch on some of these principles now. This is not nationalization. This is not the beginning of nationalization. We are not creating Crown corporations. All of the Governments involved hope their participation is temporary. We are convinced that the interests of the industry and the

November 14, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
communities which depend on them will be best served by returning the Atlantic fisheries to the private sector as soon as possible. This is our stated and explicit aim. Indeed, we would be ready to do so immediately except that at this low point in the fortunes of the industry no private investors are willing to take the risk alone.
In entering into this agreement, the Government is acutely aware of the need to consider the situation of smaller companies in the five Provinces and the way they will relate to these three new large entities. These three new companies will be among the largest fishing industry enterprises in the world, particularly those whose headquarters will be in Halifax and St. John's. They will be doing business in all four Atlantic Provinces and Quebec, which are home also to a number of much smaller independent companies. Some of these are watching developments with a certain degree of uneasiness. I understand their concern, Mr. Speaker. They want to know that this restructuring exercise, conducted after all in part with their tax dollars, will not work against their interests.
Our message to these independent companies is clear. From the start of negotiations we have kept their interests in mind. This Government believes that a vigorous and independent small business sector is indispensable to the long-term health of the Atlantic fisheries. We need a balanced mix here as much as we need it in, for instance, the airlines. The use of Government support and participation to create an unfair advantage over small and efficient companies will not be permitted. Certainly, great size will endow the new entities with new strengths, but we are taking steps to ensure that those advantages which are derived directly from size are made available to the smaller companies. One area in which size confers a strong advantage is in marketing capabilities. The three new companies would be required to make their marketing capability available on request and on mutually agreed terms to smaller independent companies.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that the action we are proposing offers the best hope we have of containing financial disaster before it spills over and engulfs the independants too. It is not hard to imagine the chaos, the shock of unemployment, economic slow-downs and the dumping of fish inventories at distressed prices which would follow a total collapse of the larger companies. This Government recognizes its responsibility to consider the social as well as the economic side of the equation. We also recognize that the new companies formed under this agreement must compete effectively in world markets. To do this they will have to plan and perform in conformity with business realities. Their decisions must make commercial sense. There is an implied division of roles and objectives here to which we give explicit recognition in this plan. If actions such as keeping a plant open that loses money are required for social reasons, then Government, not the company, will pay the cost of the action. Those companies will have to be run as efficient businesses.
We decided to follow the path I have outlined because the others, upon examination, led either nowhere or back to where we started. One such option was to make loans or guarantees to the companies in distress. This was impossible. The companies in question are incapable of carrying more debt. What is the use of more loan guarantees to those companies? They are already overburdened with debt. For obvious reasons, we rejected the use of public funds as grants to bail out shareholders and banks because there is no rationale to take taxpayers' money and give it to some companies without making the same favour to the 700 plants in eastern Canada. We cannot give grants to some when we are using taxpayers' money. As I was unable to extend that largesse to all companies, that band-aid could not be considered. It would not have gone to the root of the problem. It would have been another bail-out.
We rejected the option, if we can call it an option, of sitting passively by and watching the Atlantic fishing industry go down the drain. Such a course would be socially irresponsible and economically insane. If those companies had to go under and their huge inventories sold at distressed prices, as in any bankruptcy, it would have a domino effect of bankruptcies that would have touched and affected hundreds of other plants in eastern Canada.
The need of the hour is not only to rebuild a devastated industry but to rebuild sorely damaged confidence. The industry needs a reasonable degree of certainty about the seriousness of our commitment to restructure. The people in Atlantic fishery, fishermen, plant workers, managers, shareholders, investors, all need to know that the new structure rests on a solid base of public agreement. They need to know that the decisions made today are not subject to political shifts of the wind. We have made a strong start toward building that confidence in the agreements with Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and United Fishermen, that large important co-op in the Province of Quebec.
By coming to the House with a Bill which expresses clearly, specifically and openly what we plan to do, we build on that base. We certify that commitment with the seal of the Parliament of Canada.

It has sometimes been stated, Mr. Speaker, that periods of severe crisis were also periods of unequalled opportunity. As Arnold Toynbee suggested, a crisis is in a way a spur that stimulates healthy societies to new summits. The difficulties faced by the Atlantic fisheries already have prompted two positive responses. One is a commitment to study the underlying causes, the second is the willingness in various public and private sectors to work together to bring about changes and improvements that cannot be realized in isolation. To that extent, we can state that what appears to be a troubled period for the Canadian fishing industry can also be viewed as a period of unprecedented opportunity. This is how we are viewing the situation. We have the fish, the markets, the expertise, the willingness to work and the traditions. And now,
November 14, 1983

for the first time, we also have the means to put all those assets to intelligent use.
Before I conclude, Mr. Speaker, I would have this to add. If we seem to be viewing this legislation with some sense of urgency, it is because it is indeed a matter of urgency. Much time already has been wasted. We would have preferred debating the question in this House six months or even three months earlier. The industry has been in a difficult situation for quite some time. Each day has added its burden of economic hardship and anxiety for those in the industry. But the fact is that only a few days ago could we reach with our partners and Pecheurs-Unis in Quebec the agreement that was needed to act. As long as that agreement was not forthcoming we could not place the project before the House as long as we had no precise knowledge of what would be needed, or how much co-operation our efforts would be met with. We now have those answers, and we have a plan of action. Mr. Speaker, we know what must be done and how it must be done. 1 urge this House to deal with this Bill within the shortest possible timeframe.

Mr. Speaker, 1 thank the House for the unanimous consent. My question deals strictly with the problem of the small, independent processors. I noticed that the Minister did mention them and I will be discussing this matter later when speaking to this Bill.
