speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am very happy that my colleague, who is also Chairman of the parliamentary committee, has mentioned one particular clause of the agreement I signed with Nova Scotia. She is absolutely right. I could have told her of other very good agreements reached with the Government of Nova Scotia but the Speaker was pressing me to conclude.
The example given by the Hon. Member is one among others of things I am committed to do. The assistance I would like to give the small independent processors will go to all of them in all of Atlantic Canada. I see in the House my colleague, the Chairman of our subcommittee, the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston). We are committed to helping the independent sector in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Quebec.
This Bill will enable the Department to establish a general program that will apply to all of the industry in Atlantic Canada. As well, those companies will have to put their marketing capability at the service of the independents who request it. I am also committed to signing an agreement on development of the fisheries of Nova Scotia with the Government of Nova Scotia.
Therefore, those are some of the reasons I think it is imperative that Members, particularly of the Official Opposition, give speedy passage to this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome the opportunity this afternoon to speak to Bill C-170, an Act to authorize investment in the Atlantic fisheries for the

November 14, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
purpose of restructuring that industry. I do so more in sorrow than in anger, for the fishing industry over the years has been the hallmark of private enterprise. It was known as the one established industry which had been the hallmark of our private enterprise system and one that was established and survived because it was built upon what we in Atlantic Canada call wooden ships and iron men.
In my hometown of Lunenburg we are known as bluenosers. We carry that name with pride. We do so because it not only describes a breed of independent master mariners, it is also a name that was carried by the fastest sailing schooner in history, the Bluenose. It continues to sail on, on the back of Canada's ten-cent piece.
Our forebears worked hard to build up the fishing industry. They gave little quarter and asked for none. In the early days when codfish were caught, the fleet left port early in the New Year. The codfish were caught and brought back to port where they were dried in the sun. Later in the fall, these same codfish, now dried, were taken in the same ships that caught them out to the Caribbean where they were traded for molasses, salt, tropical fruits and sometimes even rum. Barter and trade was the order of the day. There was no thought of involving provincial or federal Governments in any of these operations, other than for the provisions of shipping and customs regulations.
All this has changed over the years. Many old mariners, or old salts as we like to call them, must be turning over in their graves today over the nationalization of Canada's fishing industry.
Despite what the Minister has stated, the Bill that is presently before the House calls for the total nationalization of the fisheries in Atlantic Canada, not just Nova Scotia or Newfoundland, but New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Quebec as well, as witnessed by the wording in the interpretation of that Act in Part II, page 2. If there are any doubts about this nationalization program, they are completely dispelled when we read of the immense powers that are being given to the Minister in paragraph 4 of page 3.
I know that the Minister does not like the nationalization term. However, the incontrovertible fact is that within one week $75 million was pledged for the fisheries in Newfoundland, and $70 million pledged for the fisheries in Nova Scotia by the federal Government alone. The provincial Governments added some $60 million and the Bank of Nova Scotia added an estimated $100 million under guarantees from the federal Government. It is no wonder that Mr. Kirby, who seems to carry more force and strength with the Government than the Minister, when commenting on what I call fisheries "mission impossible", is reported as saying, "Whatever happens now, what we have pulled off, namely restructuring the industry and at the same time creating a new federal fisheries policy, can never be undone". Is it any wonder that the private operators and Canadians generally, especially those in Atlantic Canada, are afraid?
Some people are asking when all this began. The Minister gave a good outline. According to the record on September 26, 1983, both the federal and provincial Governments in Newfoundland signed a restructuring agreement. They heralded it as the most significant agreement signed between the two Governments since Newfoundland joined Confederation in 1949. Time, Sir, alone will tell. Then on September 30, 1983, a federal-provincial agreement was announced in Port Hawkes-bury indicating both Governments would co-operate in restructuring two major Nova Scotia deep sea fishing companies. When I read both agreements I could not help but be concerned for the people of Newfoundland, for the people of Labrador and for the people of Nova Scotia. I would remind the people of both Provinces that it was the Liberals who initiated a process that led to complete federal control over the salt fishing industry in Newfoudland, and that same process led to the destruction of two or more major salt fishing companies in the Province of Nova Scotia.
It seems to me that the present group of Liberals in office have now indicated a process that will ultimately lead to the complete takeover of the fresh and frozen industry in all of Atlantic Canada as well as Quebec. I am concerned because it is obvious that this Government cannot run the railroads. It cannot run the post office. It cannot even manage its own bureaucracy. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and to this House that this Government cannot run the fishing industry because, more than with all the other industries in Canada, it requires the expertise, the initiative and the hard work of each and every individual connected with it.
The Minister may not look like the great white shark in the movie version of Jaws, but his teeth must be rather sharp because in the last few months he has gobbled up more fishing companies, enough to make Jaws look like a piker-perhaps since we are talking about fish I should say, a pike.
Both restructuring agreements contain a clause to the effect that the Governments intend to return the fishing industry to the private sector as soon as economic viability is achieved. Let me repeat, "As soon as economic viability is achieved". I would caution provincial Governments and private shareholders that granting this federal Government a major voting position on their boards of directors may introduce such inefficiencies into their companies' operations that privatization will become an ever receding goal, a mirage, a goal more difficult to attain as time goes on. If you have any doubts about that statement, Mr. Speaker, just look at what has happened to Canadair, to de Havilland, to Consolidated Computer and to other private companies taken over by this federal Government.
Our Party certainly recognizes the serious need for a restructuring of the fishing industry because many years of Liberal mismanagement have finally overwhelmed that industry and has left it no alternative. The Government is now forced to pour hundreds of millions of Canadian tax dollars into the fishery because the Government has failed, and failed miserably, to provide a consistent policy environment that
November 14, 1983

would allow private enterprise to flourish and provide meaningful jobs for Canadians.
To be factual, Canadian companies got into debt over their heads and provincial Governments licensed too many new fish plants. But I ask, who was behind it all encouraging this madcap expansion of the industry? None other than this federal Government. And if co-operative federalism had not been dead and if there had been greater consultation between federal Government and the Atlantic provincial Governments, this economic misery, heartbreak and heartache certainly could have been avoided.
With the fishery policy based more upon politics than upon sound resource management, the Liberal Government freely doled out fishing licences and it freely doled out DREE grants for plant construction and other largesse, can anyone really wonder that the Provinces, the fishermen and the companies took advantage of these handouts? So today our fishing industry is burdened with massive debts, constricted by government regulations and crippled by an inability to market all of its product.
One of the most important problems faced by Atlantic Canada's fishing industry today is, I submit, fear-fear of big government. In fact, the political influence on these new companies in Newfoundland and in Nova Scotia is today much greater than previous Government influence over the private companies. The Newfoundland super company, for example, is 85 per cent owned by Government. Eight of the 11 members of its board of directors are Government appointed. The chief executive officer is a joint appointment by both Governments. So-called significant corporate decisions are subject to the veto of the federal and provincial Governments.
Most critical of all was the fact that management must consult both Governments and the Governments consult with each other before the company's business plan may be submitted to the board of directors. Think about what 1 have just said, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure you will agree that this represents nothing more than confusion confounded.
The Minister told us of the companies he had bought out. But I ask him what did he pay the Lake group; what did he pay the Penny group; what did he pay the shareholders of Fisheries Products of Canada; what did he pay the Nickerson group for what was little more in many cases than co-operation for transferring their huge debts to the new company? Is it any wonder the secret methods that have been employed by this Government are causing independent companies and taxpayers some concern and many sleepless nights?
Throughout all of this confusion the Minister keeps saying, bragging in fact, that what he has established is not a new Crown corporation in Newfoundland or Nova Scotia. Of course, it is not. We understand that. Crown corporations have more independence than these new companies, including the ability to set up their own business plan. In a highly political industry, like the Fishing industry, this Government is more likely to be concerned about jobs and about votes than about economic viability. This is what is worrying us. We in our Party do not believe that this Government exhausted every
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act available possibility of securing equity capital, either from Canadians or from foreign interests, before nationalizing the Atlantic coast fishery. To follow this course would not fit in with this centrally minded Government that wants to control all Canadian industry. However, I am led to believe that private capital was available from Canadians-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Where?

-and from foreign countries, foreign interests, but little or no effort was made to tap these sources. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister calls out, where. I will take him aside some day and tell him something about the fishing industry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Tell the House.

Through the work of its Foreign Investment Review Agency and its ideological hostility to private industry, both foreign and domestic, this Liberal Government has ironically left the Atlantic fishery with nowhere to turn for aid but to the federal Government that helped drive it to ruin in the first place. That, to answer my young friend, is why there was no foreign capital brought forward. Take the teeth out of the Foreign Investment Review Act and then see what happens to some foreign capital. In fact, I am confident that if a proper search had been made, it would be found that Canadian capital was available. After all, we are only talking here of a couple of hundred million dollars. That is peanuts in an industry the size of the one of which we are speaking, an industry that represents to foreign nations, to European countries and to the Americans, a massive resource that has not really been tapped.
In my opinion, it is only through a fundamental shift in Government policy that stability and certainty can be returned to the fishing industry, thereby creating an environment in which free enterprise can survive. Unless this is accomplished, Sir, and I say this in all seriousness, similar problems to those which this Bill seeks to address cannot be avoided. Moreover, without the creation of a more positive business environment, private investors, either Canadian or foreign, will not risk their capital in the Canadian fishing industry. Those who remain in the industry do not believe in this Government and they do not believe that the present Liberal Government is genuinely committed to the eventual privatization of the two new restructured companies. They believe that you are only making such statements to reduce opposition to your actions and to hide your real intentions which are, in effect, in time to nationalize the entire industry.
I will give this Government a way out. In the event that it is acting in good faith and wishes to allay the fears of smaller companies and wants to make the commitment to privatization meaningful, it must establish from the very beginning a clear schedule for divesting itself of ownership in the fishery. This schedule should either be written into this Bill or at least written into agreements with the Provinces. If the Government

November 14, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act wished to take the strongest step along these lines, it could commit itself to holding only non-voting shares in these companies.
Once this step is taken, the smaller processors and fishermen would no longer have the same fears about unfair Government-controlled competition. This would also have the effect of making investment in the two companies more attractive to private investors, because the two companies would be seen as private enterprises run along sound business lines.
As private investors bought the Government's shares, they could be turned into voting shares. This would ensure that the buying out of Government shares was an attractive investment. It would also ensure that the people of Canada would recover their money. They have a stake in this too.
Another approach would be to require by law that the Government annually sell, regardless of the price, 20 per cent of its shares to the public. This would ensure that at the end of five years the two companies would be fully privatized. At the outset, the Government would not recover its investment because the share prices would be low, but under that system there would be a requirement for them to make these companies economically viable and profitable. If they did that, by the end of a five-year term the increase in equity share value would give the Government back the money it is now putting in, which is what I call pump-priming money.
At the present time, our Party intends to support this Bill at the second reading stage. However, we want to make sure that there is a full hearing on the restructuring program in committee in light of the major changes that it threatens to impose upon the Atlantic fisheries, and in fact the entire Atlantic economy. In our opinion, the Bill raises more problems than it solves.
1 thought there were only 500 independents. The Minister told us today that there were 700 independents in Atlantic Canada who do not as yet come under the socialist umbrella of this Liberal Government. They are very reticent about making public statements about the effects of this restructuring plan. They fear reprisals-imagine, reprisals from the federal Government.
I asked them what were their fears. They said that the Province grants them a licence, but the federal Government has the right to carry out dredging operations in their area. It has the right to set the fishing quotas. It has the right to determine, yes or no, whether it will repair a decrepit federal wharf which has not been repaired since 1962 when the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker was in power. They fear that if they make objection to what is being done, there will be reprisals against them in that regard. This fear demonstrates that Canadians have lost some of their basic freedoms.
At present most of these independents are relatively sound financially. They quite rightfully ask how they can compete with this monstrous tax-supported Government-financed conglomerate. The bail-outs buried in this Bill and the secret agreements are not fair and they are not above-board. The federal Government is not a minority shareholder. No matter
what this Government calls its actions, in my view it is nationalization of the fishing industry. The big unanswered question is, what is the time frame for de-nationalization? Search as you will, you will not find the answer to that question in this Bill.
It is not my intention to pre-judge entirely the outcome of the restructuring that has taken place in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. I simply wish to remind the provincial Governments, the fishermen and the industry throughout Atlantic Canada and Quebec that negotiations have really just begun. There are many pitfalls ahead. For example, 1 cannot help but wonder how the Government proposes to develop a large cooked fish production line at Burin, Newfoundland, when the present plant in my home town of Lunenburg and the one at Lachine, Quebec, can supply the total Canadian demand for cooked fish products while operating at only 50 per cent capacity.
International tariffs on cooked fish are so high at present that these products cannot be exported. 1 remind the Minister that unless you increase the market for cooked fish products, any increase in employment in Newfoundland in this field will only be at the price of further unemployment in Nova Scotia and Quebec.
This, of course, cannot be considered progress in the industry. I cannot help but wonder as well what will happen to the fishermen and the industry which evolves around the large dragger fleet based just six miles from my home town in a small place called Riverport, Nova Scotia. The Minister stated today that a new company is being formed and these ships will be transferred. I wonder as well why that action is being taken. In light of what I have said, is it any wonder that the independents and the communities in which they are located are very much concerned? They have many sleepless nights over the many aspects of this Bill. The pressure on them is already taking its toll in different forms. They ask what will be the extent of their quotas and their licences and how they will replace their aging ships.
The banks have already given the independents a signal. They have cut back on loans to independents in the fishing industry. Instead of lending them 75 per cent of their working capital, they have been told to cut their loans to 50 per cent. This is literally putting some, not all, of the independents out of business.
I ask the Minister, what is in this Bill to protect the independents? 1 have read it from cover to cover and I see nothing. They are saying that if you are going to nationalize the fishing industry, take our business now while it is worth something. The independents are comparing the Liberal actions in this Bill to those they would expect in a police state. They are asking, who is going to pick up the losses for the restructured companies? What if these companies are not privatized? What if these companies are not run on a commercially viable basis? What is the Government's definition of economic viability?
The independents are asking, since those who have been inefficient are being bailed out, what are the rewards for those
November 14, 1983

of us who have been viable? Is this to be a society where the incompetent are rewarded and the competent are penalized? 1 would like to hear the answer to that question. They ask, are you, for example, going to reform the tax legislation for independent processors and fishermen and give them a better opportunity to write off some of their valid expenses and their excessive fuel costs?
I wonder how many in this House realize that a trip from my home town of Lunenburg, to the St. Pierre area and return costs $6,000 for fuel oil. A trip from that same port to the Hamilton Bank off Labrador costs double, or $12,000 in fuel oil. There has been no change. That almost doubles the landed cost of the catch for that crew of 18 men on a 150-foot ship. When is the Government going to recognize that and give these fishermen an opportunity to write off valid expenses and their excessive costs which are driving up their costs for landing fish and lowering their net return? When some of these questions are answered either in the House or in committee, we will all have a better understanding of this Government's real plans for the future of the Atlantic fishing industry.

I would remind the Hon. Member that, although he uses partisan phrases and describes this action as a form of nationalization or socialization, this Bill results from an agreement reached between the Government of Canada, the Government of Nova Scotia and the Government of Newfoundland. I think that that is all that needs to be said. However, if we must be partisan, Mr. Speaker, and I do not suggest we should not-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: I say to the Hon. Member opposite that if he believes there to be private capital out there, I can assure him we would gladly avail ourselves of it before taking this action. Can he now tell us categorically where that private capital is?

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I believe that these last remarks constitute an abuse of a privilege extended by the House. Those remarks were debate much more than they were a question. I would be very happy to give unanimous consent to a question.

Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) and I waited as patiently as I could until he finally got around to asking his question. I regret that the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe was obviously not listening to what I said. I know that there is Canadian investment capital available and there is Japanese investment capital available to invest in the fishing industry. There is American capital that is willing to invest in the fishing industry, and those countries are afraid to invest on account of the teeth in the-
Oh, the bogeyman.

No, there is no bogey-man. The facts hurt those people opposite. They cannot stand the truth, and that is the trouble with them. I say through you, Sir, to the Members opposite that there is plenty of money available in Canada for investment in properly organized and taxed companies. However, there exists the heavy hand of the tax man who is so greedy for tax dollars that he must come down on the shares-men from a fishing crew at the rate of 60 per cent in order to get a few dollars to keep this decrepit and ailing Government operating. That is the problem, Sir. Change the Government, put us in power, and we will cut the teeth out of the Foreign Investment Review Act and see that that foreign money is invested in the fishing industry. We will privatize the industry at that time.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise and discuss what is certainly the most important fisheries legislation dealt with in this session of Parliament. The Bill has been placed before us at the end of this session and the House of Commons must deal with it with a certain amount of haste. It is a Bill of a mammoth nature that will affect Atlantic Canada and its fishing industry governed by the federal Government.
I believe that Hon. Members of all Parties understand the critical nature of a Bill that will provide $138 million to Atlantic Canada in terms of capital investment in Nova

November 14, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act Scotia, Newfoundland and the other Atlantic Provinces. However, Mr. Speaker, this Bill gives an all-encompassing power to the federal Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) when dealing with almost all aspects of federal involvement in the fishing industry and therefore gives him both direct and indirect involvement in capital funding and control over the fishing industry. This Bill really does require a great deal more attention than the Government seems to be prepared to give to it at this moment.
It is necessary to proceed with this Bill because the future of the next fishing season in Atlantic Canada relies on it. If this Bill is not passed, if there is not a restructuring of the industry and if a board of directors is not appointed to the new companies in Altantic Canada, there will be a great deal of uncertainty about markets and our ability to sell the product that is harvested over the next year. As well, the matter of negotiations between the fishermen's unions and the company for contracts in Atlantic Canada depends upon this Bill and suppliers must know whether the debts that are owed to them at the moment will be repaid. There are a great many other uncertainties in almost every community in Atlantic Canada and hundreds and hundreds of those communities are dependent upon the fishing industry.
The restructuring of the Atlantic fisheries industry through the Kirby task force was done in a great deal of secrecy. We are dealing with a Bill that arises out of a task force that was set up on January 8, 1982. It is now almost January, 1984, and we in the House of Commons are expected to deal with a Bill without a great deal of past involvement.
Hon. Members of Parliament who represent ridings in Atlantic Canada have gone through two years of uncertainty when dealing with the fishing industry. Plants have been shut down and whole communities have been out of work for over a year in some instances. We must now in the next few days deal with a restructuring Bill which requires a great deal of debate and a great deal of input from the people who are most directly involved. I would include in those concerns the concern that was expressed by the Hon. Member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) for all of the smaller independent processing companies that do not have the same kind of economic debt as the major processing companies in Atlantic Canada.
The Hon. Member for South Shore indicated that the failure of the fishing industry is mainly the responsibility of the federal Government and the Liberal Party. 1 think there is a great deal of truth to that, but there are other failings in the industry in Atlantic Canada. I think it is worth while to look at those failings to see exactly where, if we must put blame, the blame must lie.
I believe that one of the things that led to over-capitalization in the industry was the tremendous expectations of the fishing industry when the 200-mile limit was declared. There were expectations of greater access to stock and therefore greater access to processing capabilities and markets. The economic recession in the 1980s certainly contributed significantly to a reduction in the amount of product that was sold and the prices that were paid to fishermen. Management decisions led
to over-capitalization, and those included management decisions made by companies that were attempting to meet their expectations in terms of greater quantities of product and access to a great deal of federal and provincial money to expand the processing capabilities and the harvesting sector. Those expectations and offers of assistance were taken up by fishermen and processors, resulting in over-capacity both in the harvesting and the processing sectors.
I believe that at that time, both the federal and provincial Governments were attempting to create greater employment in the industry and generate greater wealth in Atlantic Canada. However, the expectations were far too high to meet the capacity of the stocks that could be produced. As much as anything else, I believe that the failure of the Atlantic fishing industry can be related to the high interest rate policies that were supported by the Liberal Government when it did not attempt to put any controls on the rate of interest that was to be paid.
Basically, the previous Government followed that policy-a rate of interest set by the Governor of the Bank of Canada which followed United States rates. Those rates themselves had a great deal of effect on how much product in terms of the groundfish resource could be sold to the United States. It soon became apparent that the expansion had gone too far. Companies may have doubled their catch but they also doubled and, in some cases, tripled their debt. Companies had paid little enough attention to increasing the quality of their catch or improving their marketing strategies. This led to a decline in the ability to sell fish and the ability to support the economics of the industry. Again I think the interest rate freeze affected expansion and was a major problem for Atlantic Canada. Companies found it necessary to switch from the goal of expansion to contraction and began to close plants. That has been going on since 1981.
Unfortunately, as always, in areas where one industry dominates, dozens of communities in Newfoundland in particular and in the Maritime Provinces were locked into the economic well-being of these large companies. They were completely reliant on the continued operation of plants and fishing operations for their own economic health. The closure of plants and fishing operations was tantamount to a death sentence for many of these communities.
The Government's response was to launch the Kirby task force, which culminated in this Bill. The process of negotiating the restructuring agreements leaves much to be desired. As I indicated earlier, there was really very little input by Members of Parliament in the restructuring. Everything was done in secrecy. This led to many suspicions between Provinces, between Provinces and the federal Government and, more important, suspicions within the communities, with plant workers and fishermen themselves. The relations among fishermen processors, plant workers, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, the provincial and federal Governments, strained at
November 14, 1983

the best of times, became more strained as a result of the way in which the negotiations were handled.
The Minister is quoted as saying that this was the hardest thing he had ever done in politics. Of course he was referring to the restructuring. I can well believe it, because as well as the incredibly serious and complex problems of the industry itself, the negotiations also had to contend with Governments that could not make up their minds on what they wanted, with one Department or Minister overruling another, with agreements signed then subsequently thrown out, with companies, especially Government-influenced companies like Fishery Products Ltd. controlled by CDC, doing everything they could to torpedo the negotiations.
Under these conditions, we are fortunate to have reached any kind of an agreement on Atlantic fisheries restructuring at this time. The fundamental difference of opinion was over the matter of priorities for the restructured companies. Some left that the number one priority should be the economic viability of the companies. Others felt that maximization of employment should take precedence. Unfortunately, I did not hear about any of the major parties taking a broad enough look at the role of the industry in the context of the economy of Atlantic Canada. They did not realize that these two objectives are not necessarily opposing forces, that depending upon one's parameters, both objectives can be achieved. It is only if one looks at the economic viability of the processing sector in isolation that it cannot include the concept of maximum employment. Unfortunately, if the company is in private hands or is intended to be returned to private hands, the only possible way it can be viewed is in isolation.
The joint agreement announced on September 26 by the Minister and Premier Peckford of Newfoundland and the subsequent agreement on September 30 with Premier Buchanan are far more responsible in this respect than the unilateral announcement of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans on July
4.
The federal Government's insistence on making economic viability its primary concern is somewhat disturbing, in face of the need in Atlantic Canada for massive employment in the fishing industry. I am pleased to see the clause in the agreement regarding the future of those plants which may be deemed uneconomic, although knowing the federal Government's attitude toward these plants in the past, the security of their future and of their communities, the clause leaves a lot to be desired. The most disturbing element of the agreements is the stated objective of returning these companies to the private sector once they have become viable. If the success of these companies is to be measured in such terms that it would be seen as viable to the private sector, then I am afraid that over time we would see the complete dominance of the concept of economic viability over maximum employment. Under the terms of the agreements, the economic viability of the company could be maintained very easily by dumping off its uneconomic elements to one or another of the Governments involved. Other companies do not have this option, so it could
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act be expected that the two new companies would certainly have a distinct advantage.
There is some question as to whether any of the other companies operating in the Maritimes or Newfoundland could stand up over time to the increasing economic and marketing dominance of these two super companies. Many of the smaller companies, as well as the Governments of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, have expressed their concern over the matter. I believe they have legitimate grounds for concern. This is a question which the Minister should address. He should give some assurance to smaller companies that they will not be forced out of the fishing industry in Atlantic Canada, particularly companies that have shown restraint and good management in their operations and have developed markets to continue ongoing employment for the communities in which they operate.
If the Government attempted to sell off its economically viable companies, would it not be essentially selling off a monopoly position in the processing sector of such an important and essential industry? There is no guarantee that both companies could not be acquired by the same buyer, nor is there any guarantee that controlling interests could not be sold to non-Canadian buyers. We in our Party would not like to see the Atlantic Canada fishing industry sold to foreign buyers, even if they were available, as the Hon. Member for South Shore seemed to indicate.
I am concerned about the position the Bank of Nova Scotia holds in these two companies. In the first place, the bank is in the business of lending money, and as such its allegiance is to its shareholders. It has little or no experience in the management of the fishing industry. It has no stake in the success of the industry in terms of the well-being of communities, only in terms of the dollar return on its investment. Yet, it has a veto power the same as that of the federal or provincial Governments when it comes to divestiture of company assets. The union, whose members have more stake in the success of the company than any of the other partners, has no such power of veto.
The Minister seems to be fairly proud of the agreements he has reached with the Provinces of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. Under this Bill he will essentially become the czar of the Atlantic fishing industry. It is all encompassing and gives almost total control to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. The Bill will give the Minister authority to "acquire, hold or dispose of or otherwise deal with shares, debentures or other securities of, or any security interest in, any fishery enterprise". In other words, the Bill does not deal just with the restructuring of major groundfish trawler companies in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia-the agreements which have already been mentioned-but it applies to every fishing enterprise on the East Coast, from the super companies to individual fishermen and everything in between.
In addition to the $138 million specifically allocated and acquired for the restructuring agreements already announced and a further $100 million available for the provision of loan guarantees, Clause 5 of the Bill indicates that the Minister

November 14, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act may, on such terms and conditions as he specifies, make a contribution or loan to a fishery enterprise with no specified limits. Thus it can be seen that with this Bill the Minister acquires almost unlimited powers to become involved in or finance virtually any fishing enterprise in eastern Canada, at his discretion and on his terms.
I have outlined many of the concerns of our Party with this Bill and with the restructuring agreements it is intended to finance. The problems I have mentioned are all potential problems. They are of concern because very few safeguards are built into either the Bill or the agreements. However, these problems do not have to arise. The key is what the Government and its partners do with the powers they have given themselves. I want to make it clear that neither the Bill nor the agreements on restructuring, nor the extensive investigations into the problems of the East Coast fishing industry, have in any way solved the problems of either the industry or the communities dependent thereon. All they have done is to keep the industry alive. The key is what happens from here.
Mention was made in the agreements of such things as the Burin Peninsula development fund, in order to find alternative sources of employment and income for the area, and the northern development fund in Newfoundland and Labrador. If such programs are not initiated quickly and managed in such a way as to produce concrete results for the people of the area- and that includes at least involving the local people in the development and operation of the program-then all of the restructuring work will have been done in vain.
The new company can provide an opportunity for community development, the involvement of the fishing industry and the plant workers. Serious attention has not been paid to marketing in Atlantic Canada to its greatest extent. The new fish company gives us that opportunity, and an opportunity to face and meet a critical factor in selling the product we produce in Atlantic Canada. More attention must be paid to fish stocks and their enhancement. This also includes protection of the habitat, both marine and freshwater, and limitation or restriction of development in areas of sensitivity to these stocks.
It is not only the processing sector which is in severe crisis. The fishermen as well are in desperate financial shape and are in need of immediate help. Such piddling programs as the $15 million Canada works program announced on November 4 by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) will not even dent the surface of the problem. It is incumbent upon the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to embark now on a program aimed at improving the financial position of the individual fisherman, giving him at least as much attention as was paid to the processing sector.
A long-term plan of action must be developed with respect to the divestiture of the assets of these two super companies if, indeed, the Government is committed to returning them to the private sector. 1 would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that once these companies have been formed, it is very unlikely that there will
be the divestiture of these companies into private hands, as the Minister indicated this afternoon. I have already pointed out the danger of simply selling these companies off in a block to the highest bidder. To maintain the social benefits of public ownership, while still complying with the free enterprise objectives of the Liberal and Tory Governments and their partner, the Bank of Nova Scotia, plans should be developed for these companies to be turned over to the communities involved, in order to allow them locally and co-operatively to own and control the companies. That is the alternative to turning those companies back to the free enterprise companies which have, partly through their own mismanagement and partly through the mismanagement of Government, failed the East Coast fishing industry and many of those communities which are dependent upon them. Communities such as Burin and Grand Bank themselves have made some initiatives to attempt to get control of their fish companies and to operate them as a co-operative with input from fishermen and plant workers in the community itself.
Our Party, rather than seeing Government investment in the fishing industry, would prefer it be turned back into private industry hands if and when these corporations become profitable and investors are again interested in investing in the Atlantic fishery. We would be far more interested in seeing the possibility of co-operatives developed within Atlantic Canada which operate and control their own fishing industry and their own employment. This, of course, would require the development of local management expertise. However, given time, this could be done through our college and university networks with the development of marine colleges and by tapping the expertise already at hand in many of the communities in Atlantic Canada.
What I am advocating is a comprehensive approach to fisheries management which sees the industry not as an isolated enterprise, which must make it or break it on its own, but rather as an integral part of the social and economic way of life in Atlantic Canada. It can provide long-term economic security as well as satisfaction and social harmony.
We understand, Mr. Speaker, the nature of this Bill and the critical time frame under which we are operating with a Bill of this kind. It is really a Bill which will save many thousands of jobs in Atlantic Canada. We are disappointed that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has not been able to present us with the Bill sooner. He has not given us an opportunity to take the Bill through committee and deal with it in a way in which we could satisfy many of our constituents in Atlantic Canada who have some serious concerns about it. We also recognize, Mr. Speaker, that there are many people in Newfoundland, in particular, who are anxiously awaiting the passage of this Bill, and our Party will not do anything which would unduly delay the passage of Bill C-170. However, we do wish the Minister would be more forthcoming in the future with the House of Commons and the Fisheries and Forestry Committee in presenting us with the opportunity to deal with Atlantic Canada and western Canadian fisheries matters in more detail.
November 14, 1983

Mr. Speaker, I do want to extend my very sincere appreciation for the consideration which has been given to me. I shall remember it and respect the Hon. Member concerned.
I suppose there is no way, Mr. Speaker, that anyone who has a distinct difference in principle with the philosophy of this Bill, can speak without being accused of being partisan. If principle and basic philosophy make me partisan, then that is what I am, and I acknowledge that before 1 begin my remarks. I am not a socialist. I do not believe for a minute that a Crown corporation of this magnitude can be established and can operate and manage more effectively and more efficiently than those who have had difficulties with the market, those who have had, for instance, generations of experience in the fishing business and who have floundered in their management practices. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, we will be hard-pressed as Hon. Members of the House of Commons, regardless of the side of the House on which we may sit, to find people with that kind of experience and knowledge of the market to make this a viable operation. From that point of view, I am partisan.
We are looking at more than 100 countries which represent possible marketing capabilities for us. We are looking at a multitude of different products, different trademarks, to which world trade has become accustomed. If we undertake a very major change in management under these circumstances, we may do more harm to our market structure than we may do good.
I look on this Bill, in reflection, as being one which might almost have come by design before this House, by choice of policy, because the policies of the Fisheries Department have not been conducive to the viability of the fishing industry at any level whatsoever. I come from a constituency in which fishing is one of the three major industries. It is not the only one, but it is one of the three major industries. I would like to give you an example of where I think the planning did not go
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
as soundly as it should have. The Government of Canada encouraged everyone to have the highest possible expectations of the impact upon our economy of the 200-mile limit and the management thereof. The Government gave DREE grants to build two herring fillet plants in Carleton-Charlotte. These two plants required a minimum of 11-inch fish to be viably processed in their filleting operations. I guess that in the 11 years it has been my privilege to be here we may have had three or maybe four years in which the supply of herring of that size was adequate to maintain full operations of those two plants and the other plants already in existence. The history of the herring industry shows that the various schools of fish which develop in that ocean do not consistently give you the size of fish necessary to make those two plants viable in the long term. So the expectation was that, with the 200 mile limit, anything we do will be viable.
I come from a constituency in which there are communities whose only source of income is the fishery. Those communities have watched Minister after Minister impose regulation after regulation. They have watched those Ministers issue additional licences for the species fished by my island constituents, to the extent that we had to impose such catch limitation on the island fishery as to make it no longer viable. We now say we have too many fishermen after too few fish, when in fact it was not that bad 15 years ago. But with the extension of fishing privileges and the division of the species among other Provinces and fishermen, the herring fleet which pioneered the industry has now been constrained by regulation to the point where its viability is questioned, even with the 200-mile limit. These are the problems facing the fishing industry, and the area I represent is finding it very difficult to remain viable under those circumstances.
So these regulations have transferred from my constituency to other areas the fishing opportunities which historically belonged to those island communities. This is because in the Minister's office and among his personnel there is the belief that any regulation applicable to the Atlantic fishery is practical for all the Atlantic fishery, but that does not apply to the outports of Newfoundland, or the East and South Coasts of New Brunswick.
We have heard from the former Minister of Fisheries and Oceans that the expectations are such that the fishermen should buy a bigger boat, make a greater effort, put more capital into the plant because there are lots of fish and we are going to nourish and nurture all species. Therefore, there will be markets and you will be rich. But in the process of developing the 200-mile limit we issued international licences and extended to the international fleet the privilege of fishing in our waters, but we did not extract in return a single improvement for ourselves in any market in the world. There might be one possible exception, that of the over-the-side sale of herring. But when we did that, we also gave additional quotas to the Russian fleet in other species, which kept our people sitting on the shore, not working.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
speechtext: Speak the facts.

I am speaking the facts. In your remarks, Mr. former Minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, indicate a single market which has been improved, as my colleague, the Hon. Member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) mentioned. Name a single market which has been improved for fillets or for cod. These things have not been improved. What happened? I agree we got larger catches, we expanded our processing capability, but we did not expand our markets, and therein lies the weakness in the policy which has brought us to this point and this legislation.
1 want to know, Mr. Speaker, why the hurry? The Government of Canada has put a gun to the head of the fishing industry of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia and said that this is the only way we will help resolve this problem. I submit that is not the way to solve anything, except, 1 suppose, in a very expensive fashion. The information I pick up is that the Provinces found themselves in such a desperate economic and social position that any proposition placed before them by the federal Government, after its mismanagement of policy, had to be accepted. I reiterate, Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend from Nova Scotia has just said, I know there were people who would have invested private money to revitalize some, if not all, of the fishing industry had it not been regulated the way it is.
1 must now come to the independents. Virtually all of the New Brunswick fishery is processed by independents except for one or two branch plants of the Nickerson family of companies which had plants in New Brunswick. These people are giving exactly the same reports as you have already heard, namely that the banks are scared of the fish processing industry, and they will only extend their credit line to the value of 50 per cent of the processors' inventory. That is a one third cut, and 1 want to ask the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. De Bane), what pressure the Government of Canada is going to put on the banks, or what substitute is it going to offer to the processors who have been treated in this fashion by the banks? The banks are scared. They may be a participant, but once burned, twice shy, and these independents need all the credit they can get to function competitively. I have suppliers to the industry who are asking me questions about whether they, as an independent oil dealer, refiner or whatever, would have an opportunity to get the business of this Crown corporation. Or will they finds themselves out in the cold without even an opportunity to compete with the Crown corporation? Call it whatever you like, but it is controlled by a Crown corporation and the five directors of the board are appointed by the Government. Will the Minister assure us that this corporation will put its business out for tender, that the little guy who has been servicing and repairing boats, or maybe the medium-sized guy, is in fact going to have the same opportunity to tender for work under this corporation? Will it be independent of Government in its allocation of benefits to the supplier to the fishing industry? That is what so many people want to know.
The Minister has said we would be able to compete with any nation in the world. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the companies competing with other nations have run afoul of a great many competitors and run afoul of duties which we are still going to have to pay. As a matter of fact, there is strong reason to believe that we may have more difficulty in trading in some parts of the world with a Crown corporation than we would have had in the private world. The moneys which the Government may be pouring into this structure may make others look at us with a rather jaundiced eye, shall we say, because of the fact it is no longer an independent private industrial competitor but, rather, a government supported competitor.
These people have been the victim of another policy of Government, namely the interest policy. Few, if any, of the small industries in Canada have been able to cope. Those who required huge inventories, in a world oversupplied with product, could not afford the 20 per cent plus interest rates which they experienced, which started the decline and the unprofitable situation in which they find themselves. It was cost of capital as well as cost of operating capital that have, to a large degree, put them in this situation.
Mr. Speaker, 1 hope that we will not have a stream of independents coming before the fisheries committee of the House of Commons saying that they have been put out of business by this huge conglomerate which has been created by Government, as came to us from the western part of Canada in the case of the freshwater fisheries. In that instance, there was no opportunity for a private dealer and little opportunity for a fisherman who did not do business with the Crown corporation. Are we going to find ourselves with another corporation financed by the Government operating under comparable principles? My fishermen are concerned about their markets through their independents. My processors are concerned about the opportunity to do business. They are wondering what additional regulation they may be facing when this conglomerate begins to function.
Mr. Speaker, on this side of the House we are faced with an ultimatum. This is the only solution which the Government of Canada offers to put fishermen, processors, processing people, marketers and transporters back into business. This is the only way. This industry was not worthy of the same consideration as the Chrysler Corporation or Massey-Ferguson or even White or Maislin. 1 am very concerned that this industry was not given comparable treatment in view of the fact that it employs many times the number of people that were employed by Ferguson, White, Chrysler and Maislin all put together. We are going to nationalize this in virtually every situation and we are going to compete with the little guy. What the opportunity will be for the little guy has not been clarified.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am partisan because my philosophy tells me that this is not the route the Government should have followed. This is a palliative which is being applied to the
